claim: TrafE is recruited to MCVs or endolysosomes in a membrane damage- or tension-dependent manner.
source: Here, we have unravelled a novel function of a TRAF-like family protein RING domain-containing E3 ligase. Among half a dozen candidates explored, we found that the evolutionary conserved E3-ligase TrafE is recruited to MCVs or endolysosomes in a membrane damage- or tension-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing TrafE recruitment to damaged MCVs and endolysosomes after LLOMe treatment or hyperosmotic shock.

claim: Five D. discoideum TRAF-like proteins (TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE) harbour all the stereotypical TRAF protein family domains.
source: Using the sequence of the human TRAF6 as a reference we searched and identified bioinformatically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) a number of D. discoideum TRAF-like proteins, five of which, namely TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE harbour all the stereotypical TRAF protein family domains, share remarkable structural similarity with human TRAF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E) and are expressed during the vegetative stage of the life cycle (Dunn et al., 2018; Stajdohar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five D. discoideum TRAF-like proteins (TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE) share remarkable structural similarity with human TRAF6.
source: Using the sequence of the human TRAF6 as a reference we searched and identified bioinformatically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) a number of D. discoideum TRAF-like proteins, five of which, namely TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE harbour all the stereotypical TRAF protein family domains, share remarkable structural similarity with human TRAF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E) and are expressed during the vegetative stage of the life cycle (Dunn et al., 2018; Stajdohar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE are expressed during the vegetative stage of the D. discoideum life cycle.
source: Using the sequence of the human TRAF6 as a reference we searched and identified bioinformatically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) a number of D. discoideum TRAF-like proteins, five of which, namely TrafA, TrafB, TrafC, TrafD, and TrafE harbour all the stereotypical TRAF protein family domains, share remarkable structural similarity with human TRAF6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E) and are expressed during the vegetative stage of the life cycle (Dunn et al., 2018; Stajdohar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2018 and Stajdohar et al., 2017.

claim: trafE is upregulated early after M. marinum infection in D. discoideum.
source: In parallel, RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) transcriptomic comparison between control and M. marinum-infected D. discoideum cells showed that out of the aforementioned candidates only trafE is upregulated early after infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Hanna et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to Hanna et al., 2019.

claim: TrafE is enriched at the early MCV as revealed by organelle proteomics.
source: TrafE is also enriched at the early MCV, as revealed by organelle proteomics (Guého et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guého et al., 2019.

claim: GFP-TrafE shows robust recruitment to MCVs as early as 1 hour post infection.
source: As early as 1 hour post infection (hpi), GFP-TrafE showed robust recruitment to MCVs, sustained over the infection time course, predominantly in the area of M. marinum bacteria poles (Figure 1A, B and C) consistent with previously demonstrated localization of ubiquitin and the autophagy-related Atg8 (López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A, B and C.

claim: GFP-TrafE recruitment to MCVs is sustained over the infection time course.
source: As early as 1 hour post infection (hpi), GFP-TrafE showed robust recruitment to MCVs, sustained over the infection time course, predominantly in the area of M. marinum bacteria poles (Figure 1A, B and C) consistent with previously demonstrated localization of ubiquitin and the autophagy-related Atg8 (López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A, B and C.

claim: GFP-TrafE recruitment to MCVs occurs predominantly in the area of M. marinum bacteria poles.
source: As early as 1 hour post infection (hpi), GFP-TrafE showed robust recruitment to MCVs, sustained over the infection time course, predominantly in the area of M. marinum bacteria poles (Figure 1A, B and C) consistent with previously demonstrated localization of ubiquitin and the autophagy-related Atg8 (López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A, B and C.

claim: GFP-TrafA remained solely cytosolic in control and infection conditions at all time points.
source: GFP-TrafA and GFP-TrafB remained solely cytosolic or nuclear, respectively, in control and infection conditions at all time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: GFP-TrafB remained solely nuclear in control and infection conditions at all time points.
source: GFP-TrafA and GFP-TrafB remained solely cytosolic or nuclear, respectively, in control and infection conditions at all time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: TrafB harbours a nuclear localization signal (NLS) similarly to human TRAF4.
source: We confirmed in silico that TrafB harbours a nuclear localization signal (NLS) similarly to human TRAF4, as predicted by both NLS Mapper and NLStradamus (Nguyen Ba et al., 2009; Kosugi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by in silico predictions using NLS Mapper and NLStradamus, with citations to the prediction tools.

claim: TrafC and TrafD are 95.56% similar in terms of amino acid sequence.
source: Interestingly, despite TrafC and TrafD being 95.56% similar in terms of amino acid sequence, they displayed different behaviour upon infection.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: GFP-TrafC was recruited to MCV during infection.
source: GFP-TrafC like GFP-TrafE was recruited to MCV, which was not the case for GFP-TrafD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: GFP-TrafD was not recruited to MCV during infection.
source: GFP-TrafC like GFP-TrafE was recruited to MCV, which was not the case for GFP-TrafD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: RT q-PCR confirmed up to fourfold upregulation of trafE at 1 hpi.
source: Real-Time quantitative-PCR (RT q-PCR) carried out to monitor the transcriptional profile in control and infected cells confirmed up to fourfold upregulation of trafE already at 1 hpi, consistent with the RNA-seq data (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Hanna et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RT q-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Intracellular growth of M. marinum WT remained unaffected in cells overexpressing TrafC.
source: Whilst the intracellular growth of M. marinum WT remained unaffected in cells overexpressing TrafC or TrafD, this growth was significantly hampered when TrafE was overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Intracellular growth of M. marinum WT remained unaffected in cells overexpressing TrafD.
source: Whilst the intracellular growth of M. marinum WT remained unaffected in cells overexpressing TrafC or TrafD, this growth was significantly hampered when TrafE was overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Intracellular growth of M. marinum WT was significantly hampered when TrafE was overexpressed.
source: Whilst the intracellular growth of M. marinum WT remained unaffected in cells overexpressing TrafC or TrafD, this growth was significantly hampered when TrafE was overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bacteria growth in the TrafE-GFP KI strain was comparable to that in WT cells.
source: Importantly, bacteria growth in the TrafE-GFP KI strain was comparable to that in WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), indicating that C-terminal GFP fusion of TrafE does not interfere with its function.
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: C-terminal GFP fusion of TrafE does not interfere with its function.
source: Importantly, bacteria growth in the TrafE-GFP KI strain was comparable to that in WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), indicating that C-terminal GFP fusion of TrafE does not interfere with its function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bacteria growth in TrafE-GFP KI cells is comparable to WT cells.

claim: Endogenous TrafE-GFP colocalized with MCVs 1.5 hr after infection.
source: In addition, the endogenous TrafE-GFP colocalized with MCVs already 1.5 hr after infection (Figure 1F) like the ectopically expressed GFP-TrafE (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The intracellular load of M. marinum-lux was increased in trafE-KO cells in a way comparable to the growth of the pathogen in autophagy-impaired atg1-KO mutant cells.
source: We observed that the intracellular load of M. marinum-lux was increased in trafE-KO cells in a way comparable to the growth of the pathogen in the autophagy-impaired atg1-KO mutant cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The endogenous amount and activity of TrafE is limiting for bacterial restriction.
source: This result, together with the decreased M. marinum growth in WT cells overexpressing TrafE (Figure 1E), indicate that the endogenous amount and activity of TrafE is limiting for bacterial restriction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that overexpression of TrafE decreases bacterial growth while loss of TrafE increases it.

claim: atg1-KO cells suffer from a complete loss of autophagy.
source: It has been demonstrated that atg1-KO cells suffer from a complete loss of autophagy resulting in the absence of xenophagy and thus were strongly impaired in the restriction of cytosolic bacteria (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: atg1-KO cells display severe developmental phenotypes and do not proceed beyond aggregation upon starvation.
source: Upon starvation, atg1-KO cells displayed severe developmental phenotypes and did not proceed beyond aggregation. In contrast, trafE-KO cells successfully completed their developmental cycle and formed viable spores (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that TrafE may not function as a general autophagy regulator but may be more specifically linked to infection- or membrane damage-related activities.
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: trafE-KO cells successfully completed their developmental cycle and formed viable spores upon starvation.
source: Upon starvation, atg1-KO cells displayed severe developmental phenotypes and did not proceed beyond aggregation. In contrast, trafE-KO cells successfully completed their developmental cycle and formed viable spores (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that TrafE may not function as a general autophagy regulator but may be more specifically linked to infection- or membrane damage-related activities.
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TrafE may not function as a general autophagy regulator but may be more specifically linked to infection- or membrane damage-related activities.
source: Upon starvation, atg1-KO cells displayed severe developmental phenotypes and did not proceed beyond aggregation. In contrast, trafE-KO cells successfully completed their developmental cycle and formed viable spores (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that TrafE may not function as a general autophagy regulator but may be more specifically linked to infection- or membrane damage-related activities.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trafE-KO cells complete development unlike atg1-KO cells, suggesting TrafE has a more specific role than general autophagy.

claim: In the absence of autophagy (e.g. in atg1-KO cells), bacteria escape the MCV precociously to the cytosol.
source: Earlier studies also indicated that in the absence of autophagy (e.g. in atg1-KO cells) or ESCRT-III-mediated membrane damage repair (e.g. in tsg101-KO cells), bacteria escape the MCV precociously to the cytosol (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: In the absence of ESCRT-III-mediated membrane damage repair (e.g. in tsg101-KO cells), bacteria escape the MCV precociously to the cytosol.
source: Earlier studies also indicated that in the absence of autophagy (e.g. in atg1-KO cells) or ESCRT-III-mediated membrane damage repair (e.g. in tsg101-KO cells), bacteria escape the MCV precociously to the cytosol (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: In trafE-KO host cells, M. marinum was exposed to the cytosol significantly earlier compared to WT cells.
source: The proportion of mCherry-Plin-positive bacteria indicated that, in trafE-KO host cells, M. marinum was exposed to the cytosol significantly earlier compared to WT cells, but similarly to atg1-KO cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Plin colocalization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In trafE-KO host cells, M. marinum was exposed to the cytosol similarly to atg1-KO cells.
source: The proportion of mCherry-Plin-positive bacteria indicated that, in trafE-KO host cells, M. marinum was exposed to the cytosol significantly earlier compared to WT cells, but similarly to atg1-KO cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Plin colocalization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In trafE-KO cells, both MCV damage repair and xenophagy restriction of bacteria are impaired.
source: Interestingly, similarly to autophagy deficient atg1-KO cells, in trafE-KO host cells M. marinum escapes earlier and displays high proliferation, suggesting that both MCV damage repair and xenophagy restriction of bacteria are impaired.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trafE-KO cells show both early bacterial escape and high proliferation.

claim: After 30 hpi, there was a significant decrease in the number of infected trafE-KO cells compared to infected WT cells.
source: Surprisingly, after 30 hpi we observed a significant decrease in the number of infected trafE-KO cells compared to infected WT cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by high-content microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After 30 hpi, there was a high number of extracellular M. marinum that had likely been released by lysis from host trafE mutant cells.
source: This was paralleled by a high number of extracellular M. marinum that had likely been released by lysis from host trafE mutant cells near 30 hpi (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by high-content microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: M. marinum is highly toxic for trafE-KO cells.
source: We confirmed that M. marinum is highly toxic for trafE-KO cells, a phenotype almost fully complemented by GFP-TrafE overexpression (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by microfluidic single-cell survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The toxicity of M. marinum for trafE-KO cells is almost fully complemented by GFP-TrafE overexpression.
source: We confirmed that M. marinum is highly toxic for trafE-KO cells, a phenotype almost fully complemented by GFP-TrafE overexpression (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by microfluidic single-cell survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The survival probability of infected autophagy-deficient atg1-KO host cells was not significantly affected during M. marinum WT infection.
source: Surprisingly, the survival probability of infected autophagy-deficient atg1-KO host cells was not significantly affected under these conditions and time-frame (Figure 2E), even though M. marinum intracellular growth is also drastically increased in these mutants compared to WT (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by microfluidic single-cell survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased cell death likely occurs later in atg1-KO compared to trafE-KO cells.
source: Increased cell death likely occurs later in atg1-KO (López-Jiménez et al., 2019) compared to trafE-KO cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to López-Jiménez et al., 2019 and inference from survival data.

claim: Absence of TrafE leads to M. marinum early escape from the MCV to the cytosol.
source: Altogether, these results reveal that as previously observed in atg1-KO cells, absence of TrafE leads to M. marinum early escape from the MCV to the cytosol, and strongly affects its targeting by the xenophagy machinery.
evidence: Supported by Plin colocalization data and bacterial growth data.

claim: Absence of TrafE strongly affects M. marinum targeting by the xenophagy machinery.
source: Altogether, these results reveal that as previously observed in atg1-KO cells, absence of TrafE leads to M. marinum early escape from the MCV to the cytosol, and strongly affects its targeting by the xenophagy machinery.
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth data and survival data.

claim: The acute toxicity of M. marinum in trafE-KO cells indicates that TrafE is more broadly involved in cell survival mechanisms compared to Atg1.
source: Importantly, the acute toxicity of M. marinum in trafE-KO cells indicates that, in contrast to Atg1, TrafE is maybe more broadly involved in cell survival mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trafE-KO cells die faster than atg1-KO cells during infection.

claim: In D. discoideum cells infected with M. marinum ∆RD1, ubiquitination of bacteria and their compartment is significantly decreased.
source: As previously shown (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017), in D. discoideum cells infected with M. marinum ∆RD1, which induces less MCV damages, ubiquitination of bacteria and their compartment is significantly decreased.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: Nearly 80% of GFP-TrafE recruitment to MCVs was observed in the vicinity of bacteria poles.
source: In addition, nearly 80% of GFP-TrafE recruitment to MCVs was observed in the vicinity of bacteria poles (Figure 1C), where ESX-1 is localized and active in both M. tuberculosis and M. marinum (Carlsson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ESX-1 is localized and active at bacteria poles in both M. tuberculosis and M. marinum.
source: In addition, nearly 80% of GFP-TrafE recruitment to MCVs was observed in the vicinity of bacteria poles (Figure 1C), where ESX-1 is localized and active in both M. tuberculosis and M. marinum (Carlsson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carlsson et al., 2009.

claim: Upon infection with M. marinum ∆RD1, TrafE-GFP recruitment to MCV was severely reduced.
source: Interestingly, upon infection with M. marinum ∆RD1, TrafE-GFP recruitment to MCV was severely reduced (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The bacteria load of M. marinum ∆RD1 was significantly and similarly reduced in both WT and atg1-KO cells.
source: Previously, we showed that both intracellular growth of WT M. marinum as well as autophagosome formation depend on a functional ESX-1 system. Consequently, the bacteria load of M. marinum ∆RD1 was significantly and similarly reduced in both WT and atg1-KO cells (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017.

claim: Lack of the ESX-1 system drastically reduced bacterial proliferation in both WT and trafE-KO cells.
source: Therefore, we measured the intracellular growth of WT and M. marinum ∆RD1 bacteria. Lack of the ESX-1 system drastically reduced bacterial proliferation in both WT and trafE-KO cells (Figure 3C), indicating that the growth advantage of WT M. marinum in trafE-KO cells is strictly dependent on MCV damage and escape to the cytosol.
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The growth advantage of WT M. marinum in trafE-KO cells is strictly dependent on MCV damage and escape to the cytosol.
source: Therefore, we measured the intracellular growth of WT and M. marinum ∆RD1 bacteria. Lack of the ESX-1 system drastically reduced bacterial proliferation in both WT and trafE-KO cells (Figure 3C), indicating that the growth advantage of WT M. marinum in trafE-KO cells is strictly dependent on MCV damage and escape to the cytosol.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ∆RD1 bacteria do not show increased growth in trafE-KO cells.

claim: The survival probability of both trafE-KO and atg1-KO host cells was not affected during infection with M. marinum ∆RD1.
source: In addition, the same microfluidic device for long-term recording of single infected cells (Figure 2E) also revealed that the survival probability of both trafE-KO and atg1-KO host cells was not affected during infection with M. marinum ∆RD1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by microfluidic single-cell survival data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Membrane damage is required for TrafE recruitment to MCVs.
source: In conclusion, we propose that membrane damage is required for TrafE recruitment to MCVs and subsequent restriction of bacteria proliferation by xenophagy.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrafE recruitment is reduced with ∆RD1 bacteria that cause less membrane damage.

claim: Membrane damage is required for subsequent restriction of bacteria proliferation by xenophagy.
source: In conclusion, we propose that membrane damage is required for TrafE recruitment to MCVs and subsequent restriction of bacteria proliferation by xenophagy.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations about TrafE recruitment, bacterial growth, and xenophagy.

claim: GFP-TrafE colocalized with K63-Ub on MCVs.
source: We carried out immunofluorescence assays using antibodies specific to K63-linkage polyubiquitin and determined that GFP-TrafE colocalized with K63-Ub on MCVs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 6 hpi, the global levels of polyubiquitination between trafE-KO and WT cells remained comparable.
source: Interestingly, at 6 hpi the global levels of polyubiquitination between trafE-KO and WT cells remained comparable (Figure 4B and C), while the fraction of K63-linkage positive MCVs was drastically reduced in trafE-KO cells (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that TrafE is involved in K63-linked polyubiquitin tagging of MCVs and bacteria.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: At 6 hpi, the fraction of K63-linkage positive MCVs was drastically reduced in trafE-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, at 6 hpi the global levels of polyubiquitination between trafE-KO and WT cells remained comparable (Figure 4B and C), while the fraction of K63-linkage positive MCVs was drastically reduced in trafE-KO cells (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that TrafE is involved in K63-linked polyubiquitin tagging of MCVs and bacteria.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: TrafE is involved in K63-linked polyubiquitin tagging of MCVs and bacteria.
source: Interestingly, at 6 hpi the global levels of polyubiquitination between trafE-KO and WT cells remained comparable (Figure 4B and C), while the fraction of K63-linkage positive MCVs was drastically reduced in trafE-KO cells (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that TrafE is involved in K63-linked polyubiquitin tagging of MCVs and bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K63-Ub levels are reduced in trafE-KO cells while total ubiquitination is not.

claim: TRAF E3-ligase activity depends on the RING domain that mediates the interaction between the E2-conjugating enzymes and their substrates.
source: It has been previously reported, that TRAF E3-ligase activity depends on the RING domain that mediates the interaction between the E2-conjugating enzymes and their substrates, and TRAF-N and RING domains-dependent homo- or hetero-oligomerizations with other members of the TRAF family (Das et al., 2021; Das et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Das et al., 2021 and Das et al., 2022.

claim: TRAF E3-ligase activity depends on TRAF-N and RING domains-dependent homo- or hetero-oligomerizations with other members of the TRAF family.
source: It has been previously reported, that TRAF E3-ligase activity depends on the RING domain that mediates the interaction between the E2-conjugating enzymes and their substrates, and TRAF-N and RING domains-dependent homo- or hetero-oligomerizations with other members of the TRAF family (Das et al., 2021; Das et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Das et al., 2021 and Das et al., 2022.

claim: Absence of the N-terminal RING domain resulted in complete loss of TrafE recruitment to MCVs throughout the infection time-course.
source: Absence of the N-terminal RING domain resulted in complete loss of TrafE recruitment to MCVs throughout the infection time-course, in contrast to the truncated TRAF-N domain version or the full-length protein (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Both truncated TrafE proteins (ΔRING and ΔTRAF-N) failed to complement the trafE-KO.
source: Despite that, functional assays using M. marinum-lux indicated that both truncated proteins failed to complement the trafE-KO (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The absence of RING domain phenocopies the truncation of the TRAF-N region because both are required for the TrafE E3 ligase activity.
source: We reason that the absence of RING domain phenocopies the truncation of the TRAF-N region because both are required for the TrafE E3 ligase activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both truncations fail to complement trafE-KO.

claim: The RING domain permits dimerization of TRAF trimers and formation of networks.
source: Additionally, the RING domain permits dimerization of TRAF trimers and formation of networks (Das et al., 2022), and also determines substrate recognition (Jackson et al., 2000) and binding to E2-conjugating enzymes, which might explain why in its absence, TrafE is not recruited to damaged MCVs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2022.

claim: The RING domain determines substrate recognition.
source: Additionally, the RING domain permits dimerization of TRAF trimers and formation of networks (Das et al., 2022), and also determines substrate recognition (Jackson et al., 2000) and binding to E2-conjugating enzymes, which might explain why in its absence, TrafE is not recruited to damaged MCVs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jackson et al., 2000.

claim: The RING domain determines binding to E2-conjugating enzymes.
source: Additionally, the RING domain permits dimerization of TRAF trimers and formation of networks (Das et al., 2022), and also determines substrate recognition (Jackson et al., 2000) and binding to E2-conjugating enzymes, which might explain why in its absence, TrafE is not recruited to damaged MCVs.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about RING domains.

claim: Minutes after treatment with 4.5 mM LLOMe, the homogenous cytosolic distribution of GFP-TrafE changed dramatically to dispersed puncta and rings.
source: Surprisingly, minutes after treatment with 4.5 mM LLOMe, the homogenous cytosolic distribution of GFP-TrafE changed dramatically to dispersed puncta and rings (Figure 6A and D, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and D.

claim: The cytosolic GFP-TrafE ∆TRAF-N was slowly recruited on the LLOMe-damaged compartments.
source: The cytosolic GFP-TrafE ∆TRAF-N was slowly recruited on the LLOMe-damaged compartments, but the cytosolic pattern of GFP-TrafE ∆RING remained unchanged until the end of the monitoring period (Figure 6B, C and D).
evidence: Supported by live microscopy data shown in Figure 6B, C and D.

claim: The cytosolic pattern of GFP-TrafE ∆RING remained unchanged after LLOMe treatment until the end of the monitoring period.
source: The cytosolic GFP-TrafE ∆TRAF-N was slowly recruited on the LLOMe-damaged compartments, but the cytosolic pattern of GFP-TrafE ∆RING remained unchanged until the end of the monitoring period (Figure 6B, C and D).
evidence: Supported by live microscopy data shown in Figure 6B, C and D.

claim: A large fraction of TrafE was recruited to Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated 10 kDa dextran-loaded endolysosomes after LLOMe treatment.
source: A large fraction of TrafE was clearly recruited to Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated 10 kDa dextran-loaded endolysosomes (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: The RING domain is essential for TrafE recruitment to damaged membranes.
source: Our data suggest that the RING domain is essential for TrafE recruitment to damaged membranes, consistent with the function of TRAF6 RING domain in formation of signalling networks (Das et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ΔRING TrafE is not recruited to damaged membranes, and supported by citation to Das et al., 2022.

claim: In WT cells, 25 min after LLOMe treatment, the lysosensor intensity first decreased but was restored to the initial level.
source: In WT cells, the lysosensor intensity first decreased but was restored to the initial level (Figure 6G and H), indicating that WT cells completed repair and recovery in the course of the 25 min of LLOMe treatment.
evidence: Supported by lysosensor fluorescence data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: WT cells completed repair and recovery in the course of the 25 min of LLOMe treatment.
source: In WT cells, the lysosensor intensity first decreased but was restored to the initial level (Figure 6G and H), indicating that WT cells completed repair and recovery in the course of the 25 min of LLOMe treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lysosensor fluorescence is restored in WT cells.

claim: In trafE mutant cells, the lysosensor fluorescence intensity remained low after LLOMe treatment.
source: In contrast, the lysosensor fluorescence intensity remained low in the trafE mutant cells (Figure 6G and H), indicating a more pronounced and perhaps irreversible proton leakage.
evidence: Supported by lysosensor fluorescence data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: trafE mutant cells show a more pronounced and perhaps irreversible proton leakage after LLOMe treatment.
source: In contrast, the lysosensor fluorescence intensity remained low in the trafE mutant cells (Figure 6G and H), indicating a more pronounced and perhaps irreversible proton leakage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that lysosensor fluorescence remains low in trafE-KO cells.

claim: Cells can fully repair damage to endolysosomes and restore their pH.
source: The results show that cells can fully repair damage to endolysosomes and restore their pH, while absence of TrafE has a strong negative impact on the integrity and the repair of damaged compartments.
evidence: Supported by lysosensor fluorescence data showing pH restoration in WT cells.

claim: Absence of TrafE has a strong negative impact on the integrity and the repair of damaged compartments.
source: The results show that cells can fully repair damage to endolysosomes and restore their pH, while absence of TrafE has a strong negative impact on the integrity and the repair of damaged compartments.
evidence: Supported by lysosensor fluorescence data showing failure to restore pH in trafE-KO cells.

claim: LLOMe-induced membrane damage reduces membrane tension similarly to hyperosmotic conditions.
source: LLOMe-induced membrane damage reduces membrane tension similarly to hyperosmotic conditions (Mercier et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2020.

claim: Water expulsion from the cytosol and from the endolysosomal compartments results in a membrane tension decrease that is sufficient to trigger the recruitment of Alix and the ESCRT-III component CHMP4B.
source: Indeed, water expulsion from the cytosol and from the endolysosomal compartments results in a membrane tension decrease that is sufficient to trigger the recruitment of Alix and the ESCRT-III component CHMP4B and subsequent formation of intralumenal vesicles (ILVs).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about membrane tension and ESCRT recruitment.

claim: Cytosolic GFP-TrafE relocated to endolysosomal compartments only seconds after the addition of sorbitol.
source: Strikingly, similarly to GFP-Vps32 (Figure 7—video 1), cytosolic GFP-TrafE also relocated to endolysosomal compartments only seconds after the addition of sorbitol.
evidence: Supported by live microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: When cells adapted and regained their initial shape and motility after hyperosmotic shock, TrafE regained a cytosolic distribution.
source: In addition, when cells adapted and regained their initial shape and motility, TrafE regained a cytosolic distribution (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by live microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Under hypertonic conditions, the lysosensor fluorescence intensity remained stable, indicating that the membrane integrity of acidic compartment was uncompromised.
source: In contrast, under hypertonic conditions, the lysosensor fluorescence intensity remained stable, indicating that the membrane integrity of acidic compartment was uncompromised (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by lysosensor fluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: A decrease of membrane tension alone is enough to trigger TrafE recruitment to endolysosomal membranes.
source: Our data suggest that a decrease of membrane tension alone is enough to trigger TrafE recruitment to endolysosomal membranes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hyperosmotic shock (which decreases membrane tension without causing damage) triggers TrafE recruitment.

claim: Cells lacking TrafE showed a highest susceptibility to LLOMe-induced sterile perforations.
source: Paralleling the results on infected cells (Figure 2E), cells lacking TrafE showed a highest susceptibility to LLOMe-induced sterile perforations (Figure 7E, Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: Supported by propidium iodide cell death assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The severity of the phenotypes caused by the absence of TrafE are a cumulative consequence of non-functional autophagy- and ESCRT-dependent membrane repair.
source: These results suggest that the severity of the phenotypes caused by the absence of TrafE are a cumulative consequence of non-functional autophagy- and ESCRT-dependent membrane repair.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trafE-KO cells show defects in both autophagy and ESCRT pathways and have more severe phenotypes than atg1-KO cells.

claim: RNA-seq comparison of trafE-KO mutant cells to WT cells revealed 283 genes with significantly differential expression.
source: RNA of trafE-KO mutant cells was collected, sequenced and compared to RNA of WT cells, revealing 283 genes with significantly differential expression (DE) (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The steady-state levels of all of the ATG-related transcripts, including atg1, atg9, atg8a and the autophagy cargo adaptors p62/sqstsm1 were clearly upregulated in trafE-KO cells.
source: Importantly, the steady-state levels of all of the ATG-related transcripts, including atg1, atg9, atg8a and the autophagy cargo adaptors p62/sqstsm1 were clearly upregulated (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The KEGG term 'autophagy-other' is significantly enriched by gene set enrichment analysis in trafE-KO cells.
source: The respective genes are listed under the KEGG term 'autophagy-other', which is significantly enriched by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: High, uncontrolled autophagy activity could be harmful for cells and may lead to accelerated cell death.
source: Earlier studies have demonstrated that high, uncontrolled autophagy activity could be harmful for cells and may lead to accelerated cell death or promote replication and spread of intracellular pathogens or cancer cells (Levine and Yuan, 2005; Ravikumar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levine and Yuan, 2005 and Ravikumar et al., 2010.

claim: High, uncontrolled autophagy activity may promote replication and spread of intracellular pathogens or cancer cells.
source: Earlier studies have demonstrated that high, uncontrolled autophagy activity could be harmful for cells and may lead to accelerated cell death or promote replication and spread of intracellular pathogens or cancer cells (Levine and Yuan, 2005; Ravikumar et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levine and Yuan, 2005 and Ravikumar et al., 2010.

claim: RNA-seq comparison between WT and trafE-KO mutant cells shows upregulation of ALIX and downregulation of its putative interacting partner Alg2A.
source: In addition, despite the fact that the read counts of the ESCRT-related genes do not show a clear overall pattern (Figure 8B), they indicate an upregulation of ALG-2-interacting-protein-X (ALIX) and downregulation of its putative interacting partner Alg2A (homolog of the human Apoptosis-linked-gene-2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Lack of TrafE alone is sufficient to affect the expression of genes belonging to the autophagy and the ESCRT families.
source: The steady-state transcriptomics comparison between WT and trafE-KO mutant cells reveals that lack of TrafE alone is sufficient to affect the expression of genes belonging to the autophagy and the ESCRT families, indicating that TrafE might function at the intersection of both ESCRT and autophagy pathways.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of autophagy and ESCRT genes.

claim: TrafE might function at the intersection of both ESCRT and autophagy pathways.
source: The steady-state transcriptomics comparison between WT and trafE-KO mutant cells reveals that lack of TrafE alone is sufficient to affect the expression of genes belonging to the autophagy and the ESCRT families, indicating that TrafE might function at the intersection of both ESCRT and autophagy pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrafE affects both autophagy and ESCRT gene expression.

claim: In D. discoideum cells, infection with M. marinum triggers an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta.
source: In D. discoideum cells, infection with M. marinum, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage or starvation trigger an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In D. discoideum cells, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage triggers an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta.
source: In D. discoideum cells, infection with M. marinum, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage or starvation trigger an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In D. discoideum cells, starvation triggers an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta.
source: In D. discoideum cells, infection with M. marinum, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage or starvation trigger an increase of LC3/Atg8 puncta (Cardenal-Muñoz et al., 2017; López-Jiménez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In WT cells, 1.5 hr after a shift to the SorMC-Sorbitol starvation medium, the number of GFP-Atg8a puncta increased.
source: As expected in WT cells, 1.5 hr after a shift to the SorMC-Sorbitol starvation medium, the number of GFP-Atg8a puncta increased and to our surprise in trafE-KO cells the number of structures was significantly higher than in WT cells (Figure 9A and B), indicating that TrafE is apparently not required for autophagy initiation.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: In trafE-KO cells, 1.5 hr after a shift to the SorMC-Sorbitol starvation medium, the number of GFP-Atg8a structures was significantly higher than in WT cells.
source: As expected in WT cells, 1.5 hr after a shift to the SorMC-Sorbitol starvation medium, the number of GFP-Atg8a puncta increased and to our surprise in trafE-KO cells the number of structures was significantly higher than in WT cells (Figure 9A and B), indicating that TrafE is apparently not required for autophagy initiation.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: TrafE is apparently not required for autophagy initiation.
source: As expected in WT cells, 1.5 hr after a shift to the SorMC-Sorbitol starvation medium, the number of GFP-Atg8a puncta increased and to our surprise in trafE-KO cells the number of structures was significantly higher than in WT cells (Figure 9A and B), indicating that TrafE is apparently not required for autophagy initiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atg8a puncta still form (and even accumulate) in trafE-KO cells during starvation.

claim: Upon generation of sterile damage, trafE-KO cells exhibited a lower number of GFP-Atg8a structures compared to WT cells.
source: In contrast, upon generation of sterile damage, trafE-KO cells exhibited a lower number of GFP-Atg8a structures compared to WT cells (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The absence of TrafE in cells treated with LLOMe lead to accumulation of large Atg8a-positive crescent-like structures.
source: Notably, the absence of TrafE in cells treated with LLOMe lead to accumulation of large Atg8a-positive crescent-like structures (Figure 9D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Accumulation of Atg8/LC3 structures occurs in yeast and mammalian cells lacking or expressing dominant-negative forms of ESCRT subunits required for autophagosome biogenesis, closure and maturation.
source: This phenotype is reminiscent of the accumulation of Atg8/LC3 structures in yeast and mammalian cells lacking or expressing dominant-negative forms of ESCRT subunits required for autophagosome biogenesis, closure and maturation (Takahashi et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2018 and Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: The D. discoideum E3-ligase TrafE acts downstream of Atg1 in the autophagy pathway.
source: Our data suggest that the D. discoideum E3-ligase TrafE acts downstream of Atg1 in the autophagy pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that autophagy is initiated in trafE-KO cells but structures accumulate.

claim: The accumulation of Atg8a puncta in starved trafE-KO cells is likely a consequence of a partial impairment but not a complete block of autophagy flux.
source: The accumulation of Atg8a puncta in starved trafE-KO cells is likely a consequence of a partial impairment but not a complete block of autophagy flux, because trafE-KO cells complete their developmental cycle unlike the fully autophagy deficient atg1-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trafE-KO cells complete development while atg1-KO cells do not.

claim: In mammalian and D. discoideum cells, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage triggers vigorous recruitment of ALIX to damaged endolysosomal compartments.
source: In mammalian and D. discoideum cells, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage triggers vigorous recruitment of the ESCRT subunits involved in membrane scission, ALIX and CHMP4B/Vps32, to damaged endolysosomal compartments (López-Jiménez et al., 2018; Mercier et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In mammalian and D. discoideum cells, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage triggers vigorous recruitment of CHMP4B/Vps32 to damaged endolysosomal compartments.
source: In mammalian and D. discoideum cells, LLOMe-induced sterile membrane damage triggers vigorous recruitment of the ESCRT subunits involved in membrane scission, ALIX and CHMP4B/Vps32, to damaged endolysosomal compartments (López-Jiménez et al., 2018; Mercier et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 redistribution from the cytosol to damaged, dextran-positive, compartments was significantly more pronounced in trafE-KO compared to WT cells.
source: Most surprisingly, ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 redistribution from the cytosol to damaged, dextran-positive, compartments was significantly more pronounced in trafE-KO compared to WT cells (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 10C and D.

claim: In WT and trafE-KO cells starved for 1.5 hr, both ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 redistributed to a high number of dextran-negative foci and structures.
source: In order to further dissect the functionality of the recruited subunits, the behaviour of these ESCRT reporters was monitored in starvation conditions. In WT and trafE-KO cells starved for 1.5 hr, both ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 redistributed to a high number of dextran-negative foci and structures (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that the ESCRT machinery components are recruited to autophagosomes.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The ESCRT machinery components are recruited to autophagosomes during starvation.
source: In order to further dissect the functionality of the recruited subunits, the behaviour of these ESCRT reporters was monitored in starvation conditions. In WT and trafE-KO cells starved for 1.5 hr, both ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 redistributed to a high number of dextran-negative foci and structures (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that the ESCRT machinery components are recruited to autophagosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ALIX and Vps32 localize to dextran-negative structures during starvation, and this is autophagy-dependent.

claim: In starved autophagy initiation-deficient atg1-KO cells, there was no corresponding increase of ALIX-GFP or GFP-Vps32 structures.
source: This hypothesis was confirmed by the lack of a corresponding increase of ALIX-GFP or GFP-Vps32 structures in starved autophagy initiation-deficient atg1-KO cells (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: In starved trafE-KO cells, the number of both ALIX-GFP or GFP-Vps32 foci and structures was significantly higher relative to WT cells.
source: Remarkably, in starved trafE-KO cells, the number of both ALIX-GFP or GFP-Vps32 foci and structures was significantly higher relative to WT cells (Figure 10—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The excessive accumulation of ESCRT components on damaged endolysosomes or autophagy-related structures observed in trafE-KO cells might reflect an incomplete engagement of both ESCRT and autophagy machineries.
source: The excessive accumulation of ESCRT components on damaged endolysosomes or autophagy-related structures observed in trafE-KO cells might reflect an incomplete engagement of both ESCRT and autophagy machineries, thereby placing TrafE at their intersection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ESCRT components accumulate but repair is impaired in trafE-KO cells.

claim: The Vps4 ATPase is essential for the assembly, the disassembly and the dynamic turnover of ESCRT-III subunits during MVB formation and membrane remodelling.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the Vps4 ATPase is essential for the assembly, the disassembly and the dynamic turnover of ESCRT-III subunits during MVB formation and membrane remodelling, and that the absence of Vps4 leads to accumulation of ESCRT components on endosomes (Shestakova et al., 2010; Mierzwa et al., 2017), formation of Atg8 clusters and defects in autophagosome closure (Takahashi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The absence of Vps4 leads to accumulation of ESCRT components on endosomes.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the Vps4 ATPase is essential for the assembly, the disassembly and the dynamic turnover of ESCRT-III subunits during MVB formation and membrane remodelling, and that the absence of Vps4 leads to accumulation of ESCRT components on endosomes (Shestakova et al., 2010; Mierzwa et al., 2017), formation of Atg8 clusters and defects in autophagosome closure (Takahashi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The absence of Vps4 leads to formation of Atg8 clusters and defects in autophagosome closure.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the Vps4 ATPase is essential for the assembly, the disassembly and the dynamic turnover of ESCRT-III subunits during MVB formation and membrane remodelling, and that the absence of Vps4 leads to accumulation of ESCRT components on endosomes (Shestakova et al., 2010; Mierzwa et al., 2017), formation of Atg8 clusters and defects in autophagosome closure (Takahashi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2018.

claim: After addition of 4.5 mM LLOMe in WT cells, GFP-Vps4 was robustly redistributed from the cytosolic pool to damaged endolysosomes.
source: As expected (López-Jiménez et al., 2018), after addition of 4.5 mM LLOMe in WT cells, GFP-Vps4 was robustly redistributed from the cytosolic pool to damaged endolysosomes.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data and citation to previous work.

claim: In trafE-KO cells, the recruitment of GFP-Vps4 to endolysosomal damage sites was abolished.
source: In striking contrast, in trafE-KO cells the recruitment of GFP-Vps4 to endolysosomal damage sites was abolished (Figure 11A and B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 11A and B.

claim: The Vps4 recruitment defect in trafE-KO cells was reversed by re-expression of mRFP-TrafE.
source: This phenotype was reversed by re-expression of mRFP-TrafE in GFP-Vps4 expressing trafE-KO cells (Figure 11—figure supplement 1), and mRFP-TrafE colocalized with Vps4 on damaged endolysosomes (Figure 11D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: mRFP-TrafE colocalized with Vps4 on damaged endolysosomes.
source: This phenotype was reversed by re-expression of mRFP-TrafE in GFP-Vps4 expressing trafE-KO cells (Figure 11—figure supplement 1), and mRFP-TrafE colocalized with Vps4 on damaged endolysosomes (Figure 11D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: Absence of the E3-ligase TrafE impairs Vps4 recruitment to damage sites where ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 accumulation results in non-functional ESCRT-mediated repair.
source: We conclude that absence of the E3-ligase TrafE somehow impairs Vps4 recruitment to damage sites where ALIX-GFP and GFP-Vps32 accumulation results in non-functional ESCRT-mediated repair.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vps4 is not recruited while ALIX and Vps32 accumulate in trafE-KO cells.

claim: ALIX binding to K63-Ub chains establishes a positive feedback loop resulting in the stimulation of Vps4 activity.
source: Previous studies have linked ALIX binding to K63-Ub chains with the establishment of a positive feedback loop resulting in the stimulation of Vps4 activity.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about ALIX-ubiquitin interactions.

claim: Failure of Vps4 to interact with Ub-bound ALIX results in major defects in cargo sorting.
source: It was demonstrated that failure of Vps4 to interact with Ub-bound ALIX results in major defects in cargo sorting (Pashkova et al., 2013; Tseng et al., 2021; Pashkova et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: D. discoideum ALIX contains a likely ubiquitin binding domain (UBD).
source: Comparison of D. discoideum ALIX with a group of structurally defined but evolutionary distant coiled-coil Ubiquitin Binding Domain (UBD)-containing proteins revealed the presence of highly conserved residues, indicating a likely UBD (Figure 12—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: In LLOMe-treated WT cells, ALIX-GFP was robustly redistributed to damaged compartments where it colocalized with K63-linked polyubiquitin.
source: As expected, compared to mock-treated, LLOMe-treated WT and atg1-KO cells revealed a robust redistribution of cytosolic ALIX-GFP to damaged compartments where it colocalized with K63-linked polyubiquitin (Figure 12A, C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 12A, C, D and E.

claim: In LLOMe-treated atg1-KO cells, ALIX-GFP was robustly redistributed to damaged compartments where it colocalized with K63-linked polyubiquitin.
source: As expected, compared to mock-treated, LLOMe-treated WT and atg1-KO cells revealed a robust redistribution of cytosolic ALIX-GFP to damaged compartments where it colocalized with K63-linked polyubiquitin (Figure 12A, C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 12A, C, D and E.

claim: TrafE mutants displayed the usual high number of ALIX-GFP structures in both the mock- and the LLOMe-treated conditions.
source: Remarkably, TrafE mutants displayed the usual high number of ALIX-GFP structures in both the mock- and the LLOMe-treated conditions, however the K63-linked ubiquitination of damaged compartments was virtually abolished (Figure 12B, D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 12B, D and E.

claim: In TrafE mutants, the K63-linked ubiquitination of damaged compartments was virtually abolished.
source: Remarkably, TrafE mutants displayed the usual high number of ALIX-GFP structures in both the mock- and the LLOMe-treated conditions, however the K63-linked ubiquitination of damaged compartments was virtually abolished (Figure 12B, D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 12B, D and E.

claim: The D. discoideum E3-ligase TrafE is responsible for K63-linked polyubiquitination of MCV or endolysosomal membrane protein(s) upon damage triggered by perforation-induced changes in membrane.
source: We conclude that the D. discoideum E3-ligase TrafE is responsible for K63-linked polyubiquitination of MCV or endolysosomal membrane protein(s) upon damage triggered by perforation-induced changes in membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K63-Ub levels are drastically reduced in trafE-KO cells on damaged compartments.

claim: In WT cells, TrafE-dependent ubiquitination of unknown endolysosomal membrane protein(s) with K63-polyubiquitin promotes K63-Ub-ALIX interaction which enhances ALIX ability to stimulate Vps4 activity.
source: According to our working model in WT cells (Figure 13A), ALIX, Vps32 and TrafE are recruited to small size damage sites. TrafE-dependent ubiquitination of unknown endolysosomal membrane protein(s) with K63-polyubiquitin promotes K63-Ub-ALIX interaction which enhances ALIX ability to stimulate Vps4 activity and triggers its functional recruitment to damage sites resulting in proper ESCRT-III turnover.
evidence: This is a working model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: TrafE-deposited K63-Ub may serve as a signal for the recruitment of the autophagy adaptor p62 and the autophagy machinery in case of substantial damage.
source: In case of substantial damage, it is possible that TrafE deposited K63-Ub serves as a signal for the recruitment of the autophagy adaptor p62 and the autophagy machinery leading to formation of a phagophore-like structure which seals by membrane fusion the damage site.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: In atg1-KO cells, the ESCRT-dependent damage repair is functional.
source: In atg1-KO cells (Figure 13B), the ESCRT-dependent damage repair is functional, however the cells are autophagy deficient and therefore there is no formation of phagophore and no autophagy-dependent fusion-type membrane repair.
evidence: This is a model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: In trafE-KO cells, the absence of K63-Ub impairs the autophagy-dependent fusion-type repair.
source: In parallel, the absence of K63-Ub also impairs the autophagy-dependent fusion-type repair which altogether explains the severity of the trafE-KO phenotypes compared to atg1-KO mutant cells.
evidence: This is a model based on inference from experimental data.

claim: TrafE may be involved in phagophore closure.
source: Based on recent studies revealing the function of the ESCRT machinery in phagophore closure (Takahashi et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2019; Zhen et al., 2020), we speculate that TrafE may also be involved in this process (Figure 13D).
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from experimental data and citations to previous work.
